LI2026EE.title: One market, two logics: Salience and asymmetric myopia in China's vehicle choices
collections: 用户项目直接对话文献（不在 2026-03-21 Zotero 语料内）
LI2026EE.classification: canonical BLP demand（随机系数 logit + 分动力不注意参数）

apa_citation.reference: Li, Z. (2026). One market, two logics: Salience and asymmetric myopia in China's vehicle choices. Energy Economics, 158, 109377. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.eneco.2026.109377

LI2026EE.card_provenance: 本卡由 Claude 于 2026-08-26 直接读原 PDF（15 页）逐节建立；数值均从原文表格与正文抄录并复算，非语料自动生成。

note_sections.1. One-paragraph thesis: 把能源悖论从'消费者是否统一理性'推进到'不同动力类型是否被同等注意'。用 2022-06 至 2025-06 车型—城市—月抓取面板（1,146,659 观测）估计随机系数 logit，把不注意参数按动力类型分解为 γ_conv 与 γ_diff，发现 ICEV 买家对未来能源支出打折、NEV 买家接近甚至超过完全资本化。机制归因于显著性驱动的注意力配置：醒目的购车价挤占对未来成本的注意，反之亦然。
note_sections.2. Story ladder: 现实张力：购车是典型的跨期权衡，但标准模型假定统一理性 → 缺口：能源悖论文献几乎都估一个统一的不注意参数，掩盖了动力类型之间的差别 → 本文动作：把不注意参数写成 γ_conv + γ_diff·D_NEV 的嵌套结构，直接可检验 → 收益：福利损失主要来自 ICEV 买家的短视，因而定向信息干预是广谱补贴的有效补充。
note_sections.3. Model or identification core: 效用 u_ijt = x_jt β^x_i − α_i[p_jt + (γ_conv,i + γ_diff,i·D_jt) G_jt] + ξ_jt + ε_ijt。关键在于 γ 写在方括号内，因而它直接就是资本化比率，不需要事后做 γ/α。ξ_jt = ξ_j(细分市场FE) + ξ_t(地区与年月FE) + ξ̃_jt。价格内生用成本移子工具：大宗商品期货 VWAP × 车型静态属性（把每种原材料匹配到决定其用量的具体属性）。
note_sections.4. Data and measurement: 抓取汽车之家、懂车帝、16888.com 三个门户；车型—城市—月，2022-06 至 2025-06；1,146,659 观测（ICEV 782,919 / NEV 363,740）。消费者异质性由 2020 人口普查县级数据 + CEIC/CNRDS/CSMAR 模拟，无个体买家微观数据。能源价格：汽柴油走国家调价机制，公共充电费率来自 m.icauto.com.cn。
note_sections.5. Findings and mechanisms: RCL 列：γ_conv = 0.8005 (0.1942)，γ_diff = 0.3661 (0.1124)，γ_NEV = 1.1666 (0.2533)。★星号是对 0 的检验：对经济基准 1 而言 (0.8005−1)/0.1942 = −1.03、(1.1666−1)/0.2533 = 0.66，两者均不显著异于 1；有统计支持的只有两者之差。机制：显著性指数 S_jt = |x_jtk − x̄_k| / (|x_jtk| + |x̄_k| + ε)，三种参考点情景（老练买家/ICEV 锚定新手/无偏购物者），三重交互 S×G×NEV 检验注意力挤占。
note_sections.6. Contribution construction: 空白：现有能源悖论文献用统一不注意参数。动作：嵌套分解 γ_conv + γ_diff·D，避免 ad-hoc 系数比较。收益：福利分解显示损失主要来自 ICEV 侧，政策含义从'补贴 NEV'转向'给 ICEV 买家做信息干预'。
note_sections.7. Literature review function: 围绕两条线组织：能源悖论与不注意（Allcott 2013、Allcott-Wozny 2014、Grigolon et al. 2018、Gillingham et al. 2021、Levinson-Sager 2023），以及显著性理论（Bordalo-Gennaioli-Shleifer 2012/2013、Chetty-Looney-Kroft 2009、Brown-Hossain-Morgan 2010）。方法谱系引 BLP 1995、BLP 2004、Conlon-Gortmaker 2020。
note_sections.8. Writing structure map: 引言（跨期权衡→注意力竞争→ICEV vs NEV 对比）→ 概念框架（结构方法、效用、异质性、份额加总）→ 抓取数据与变量 → 估计与识别（内生性与工具、参数识别、计算）→ 实证（基准不对称短视、人口异质性、稳健性与替代解释、显著性机制、反事实与福利）→ 讨论。
note_sections.9. Reusable writing moves: 把'统一参数'写成需要放松的限制而不是技术细节；用嵌套分解替代系数比较以获得直接可检验的结构；把福利分解落到'损失来自哪一侧'而不是总量。
note_sections.10. Memory update: 本项目最直接的对话对象与竞争者。增量必须来自制度冲击（工况口径改革提供预定的、车型异质的信息冲击），而不是延长样本或再估一次两类成本系数。

LI2026EE.theory_design_memory: 研究设计类型：结构需求估计 + 显著性机制检验 + 福利反事实。模型类：随机系数 logit（BLP），非线性参数 θ2 = (Π, Σ)。核心创新：不注意参数按动力类型嵌套分解 γ_i = γ_conv,i + γ_diff,i·D_jt，写在 α_i 的方括号内因而直接是资本化比率。随机系数 β_i = (α_i, β^x_i, γ_conv,i, γ_diff,i)' = 均值 + Π d_i + Σ ν_i，ν ~ N(0,I)。δ/μ 分解见 (5)-(8)，其中 μ(3) = −G_jt(τ_conv,i − τ̄_conv)、μ(4) = −D_jt G_jt(τ_diff,i − τ̄_diff)，注意 γ 与 α 是乘性纠缠的（τ ≡ αγ）。识别策略：成本移子工具（大宗商品期货 VWAP × 车型静态属性）解决价格内生。承重假设：随机游走的燃油价格预期 E[g_ts] = g_t；能效 e_j 为车型固定参数；寿命 S = 10 年、贴现 r = 6%。
LI2026EE.baseline_core_memory: 基准回归是 Table 4 三列并列：(1) IV Logit、(2) Restricted RCL、(3) RCL。因变量是市场份额（车型—城市—月），观测 1,146,659。Panel A 均值效用：Price(α) −0.0894***/−0.0941***/−0.1011***；G_jt(α·γ_conv·ρ) −0.4807***/−0.4756***/−0.5955***；G_jt×NEV(α·γ_diff·ρ) −0.9031***/−0.9324***/−0.2723***；NEVs(β^x_1) 0.1718***/0.1753***/−2.6903***；进口车 −0.79 左右；整备质量、车载空气净化器、卫星导航为控制属性。Panel B 随机系数标准差：Price(Σ_α) − / 0.0000 / 0.0010(0.8451)；NEVs(Σ_x) − / 0.0000 / 2.5828***。Panel C 由 Panel A 反算的估值参数：ICEVs(γ_conv) 0.7308***/0.6866***/0.8005***；Difference(γ_diff) 1.3730***/1.3461***/0.3661***；NEVs 2.1038***/2.0327***/1.1666***。固定效应：车型细分 + 购买时间 + 购买地点，三者可加而非交互。标准误在市场层（城市×年月）聚类。★★ RCL 列一放开异质性，不注意参数标准误从 0.06 跳到 0.19–0.25，而价格随机系数 Σ_α = 0.0010 (0.8451) 完全测不准、NEV 随机系数却 2.5828***，说明该列异质性几乎全落在 NEV 品味上，γ 与 NEV 随机系数分离得很弱。
LI2026EE.mechanism_memory: 机制章节走显著性理论。定义显著性 S_jtk(x_jtk, x̄_k) = |x_jtk − x̄_k| / (|x_jtk| + |x̄_k| + ε)，分子是对比效应、分母做归一化、ε 保证有界并满足敏感性递减。构造两个指数：前端成本显著性 S^P（用购车价，是经销商处的'贴纸信息'，无需心算）与未来成本显著性 S^G（用预期生命周期能源支出 G_jt，通过能耗标识或销售话术被注意到）。参考点 x̄_k 分三种情景：老练买家（历史全国 ICEV 价格）、ICEV 锚定新手（当地当期传统燃油车）、无偏购物者（当地当期全部可选车型含 NEV）。用三重交互 S_jt × G_jt × NEV 检验注意力挤占：醒目的前端价格挤占对未来成本的注意，反之长期节省也会分散对购车价的注意。异质性章节按人口特征（收入、教育、城市层级）分层报告不对称短视的差异。
LI2026EE.result_memory: 摘要口径：ICEV 买家平均只愿为 1 单位折现未来能源节省支付 0.80 单位购车价；NEV 买家为 1.17。★该表述在 RCL 列缺乏对基准 1 的统计支持，只有 γ_diff = 0.3661 (0.1124, t≈3.26) 显著。描述统计（Table 1）：预期燃料成本 ICEV 0.4999 vs NEV 0.2132（十万元），燃料消耗 ICEV 6.83 L/100km、NEV 1.27 L/100km，电耗 NEV 14.32 kWh/100km，整备质量 ICEV 1.59t vs NEV 1.79t，价格 ICEV 1.85 vs NEV 1.71（十万元）。稳健性：替代贴现率与寿命、复合充电习惯与滚动窗口油价预期、多起点 GMM 检验全局最优、地方能源价格内生性的 IV 处理。福利：决策效用 Ṽ 用有偏 γ、经验效用 V* 固定 γ = 1；信念误差 V^b = α_i[1 − (γ_conv,i + γ_diff,i D_jt)]G_jt；决策消费者剩余 CS^d = ∫ (1/α_i) ln(1 + Σ_j exp Ṽ_ijt) dF(θ_i)；市场层信念误差 CS^b = ∫ (Σ_j P_ijt(Ṽ)·[1 − (γ_conv,i + γ_diff,i D_jt)]G_jt) dF(θ_i)。结论是福利损失主要来自 ICEV 买家的短视。
LI2026EE.writing_style_memory: 摘要用'把 X 推进到 Y'的结构：把能源悖论从统一理性推进到不对称短视。引言第一段用跨期权衡的经典张力开场，第二段引入注意力竞争这一自下而上的过程，第三段说明 ICEV 与 NEV 的对比使该机制格外可见。模型章节先讲'为什么不用 Cobb-Douglas'（脚注 1：耐用品 p/y 不可忽略，线性近似丢曲率；且拟线性使 BLP 反演与福利计算数值稳定），这种把设定选择写成正面论证而非默认的写法值得学。福利章节明确区分决策效用与经验效用并沿用 Allcott (2013) 的框架。

intro.snippet:
yopia in Vehicle Purchases: Evidence from a Natural Experiment
text
Kenneth Gillingham, Sébastien Houde, and Arthur van Benthem
text
NBER Working Paper No. 25845
text
May 2019
text
JEL No. D12,L62,Q4
ABSTRACT
A central question in the analysis of fuel-economy policy is whether consumers are myopic with regards to future fuel costs. We provide the first evidence on consumer valuation of fuel economy from a natural experiment. We examine the short-run equilibrium effects of an exogenous restatement of fuel-economy ratings that affected 1.6 million vehicles. Using the implied changes in willingness-to-pay, we find that consumers act myopically: consumers are indifferent between $1 in discounted fuel costs and 15-38 cents in the vehicle purchase price when discounting at 4%. This myopia persists under a wide range of assumptions.

estimates centered around one, implying that consumers fully value future fuel savings. Busse, Knittel, and Zettelmeyer (2013) also rely on gasoline price variation and use both new and used vehicle data, while Sallee, West, and Fan (2016) estimate their model with used vehicle auction data and use variation in odometer readings. Grigolon, Reynaert, and Verboven (2018) use temporal variation in gasoline prices combined with cross-sectional variation in engine technology to find a central-case valuation parameter of 0.91 in Europe. Taken together, these studies suggest modest undervaluation at most.6 In contrast, Leard, Linn, and Zhou (2018) use data from new vehicles in the United States and exploit the timing of adoption of fuel-saving technologies. They find a substantially lower valuation parameter of 0.54. Leard, Linn, and Springel (2019) focus on using cross-sectional variation in engine technologies and find even lower values; most of their estimates are below 0.30.

model.snippet:
by the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA), the two major automakers Hyundai and Kia acknowledged that they had overstated the fuel economy for 13 important vehicle models from the 2011- 2013 model-years by one to six miles-per-gallon. This overstatement—by far the largest in history—affected over 1.6 million vehicles sold, including several popular models such as the Hyundai Elantra and Kia Rio. Hyundai and Kia blamed a “procedural error” in the mileage testing and had to abruptly change the official fuel-economy ratings for these vehicles. Following the restatement, the automakers agreed to compensate buyers who had already purchased vehicles with misstated ratings, while new car buyers after the restatement did not receive compensation.4 The restatement was unexpected—even just prior to it, Hyundai and Kia often advertised the high fuel economy of their vehicles as a major selling feature.

results.snippet:
n the equilibrium prices of the affected models (just under $300). We then proceed by directly estimating the consumer valuation of fuel economy. Using our preferred set of valuation assumptions, our results indicate that consumers are indifferent between one dollar in future gasoline costs and 15-38 cents in the vehicle purchase price (a ‘valuation parameter’ of 0.15-0.38) depending on the affected model-year, and using a discount rate of 4%. We thus find that consumers systematically undervalue fuel economy in vehicle purchases to a larger degree than reported by much of the recent literature. This conclusion is robust to a wide range of valuation assumptions, including vehicle supply elasticities, as we illustrate in a bounding exercise.

note_sections.1. One-paragraph thesis:
- The paper asks whether the energy efficiency gap in refrigerators is driven by consumer myopia and imperfect competition.
- It finds that consumers do undervalue future energy savings, but the resulting energy-use effect is modest.
- The broader implication is that the gap exists, but this market's inefficiency is smaller than the strongest behavioral stories suggest.
note_sections.2. Story ladder:
- Real-world tension or puzzle: energy-efficient appliances often do not sell as much as engineering calculations imply they should.
- Why the puzzle matters now: policy debates hinge on whether the gap is behavioral, market-power driven, or both.
- What the literature already explains: myopia and imperfect competition are both plausible explanations.
- What is still missing or weakly identified: a market-level decomposition of how much each channel actually matters.
- The paper's move: estimate demand and counterfactuals in the UK refrigerator market.
- Main payoff: myopia matters, but not enough to explain the whole gap.
note_sections.3. Model or identification core:
- Research design type: structural demand and counterfactual analysis.
- Structural model class or reduced-form design: refrigerator choice model with energy costs and imperfect competition.
- Key equations or choice objects: consumer utility over purchase price, operating cost, and product attributes.
- Endogeneity problem: observed prices and qualities reflect firm strategic pricing and consumer preferences.
- Identification strategy: infer willingness to pay and discounting from observed product choices and market structure.
- What assumptions are doing the heavy lifting: stable demand, credible fuel-cost expectations benchmark, and firm pricing behavior.
note_sections.4. Data and measurement:
- Unit of observation: refrigerator products / market shares in the UK.
- Market definition: UK refrigerator retail market.
- Main dependent variable: product choice and implied energy consumption.
- Core explanatory variables: purchase price, operating cost, energy label / efficiency, and competition structure.
- Instruments / moments / shocks: not fully extracted from OCR; likely product market moments rather than a single external instrument.
- Important sample restrictions: refrigerator market only; precise sample window was not fully recoverable from OCR.
note_sections.5. Findings and mechanisms:
- Baseline result: average energy consumption is only about 7.2% higher than the perfect-competition, non-myopic benchmark.
- Mechanism evidence: consumers underestimate future energy savings by about 35%.
- Heterogeneity evidence: the myopia channel exists, but its aggregate effect is smaller than many policy arguments imply.
- Welfare or counterfactual result: imperfect competition lowers energy use somewhat, but the gap remains.
- Limits the authors admit: the paper is one market and one product category, so generalization should be cautious.
note_sections.6. Contribution construction:
- Which papers are treated as the nearest neighbors: energy-efficiency-gap, myopia, and imperfect competition papers.
- What exact gap the authors claim: prior work often identifies a gap, but not its quantitative magnitude in a real market.
- How the introduction stages novelty: by combining behavioral discounting with market structure in a structural setup.
- Whether the contribution is data, method, theory, policy, or a combination: mainly method plus policy-relevant quantification.
note_sections.7. Literature review function:
- Where the review sits: early introduction, before the structural model.
- How the review is organized: behavioral explanations, market-power explanations, and appliance-efficiency evidence.
- Which citations do positioning work: energy-efficiency-gap and consumer myopia studies.
- Which citations do method-validation work: structural demand and industrial-organization papers on product markets.
note_sections.8. Writing structure map:
- Introduction move sequence: puzzle -> candidate explanations -> empirical gap -> market study -> result.
- Section order: background, model, data, estimation, counterfactuals, conclusion.
- Where the paper turns from setup to payoff: once the benchmark comparison shows the gap is smaller than expected.
- How tables/figures are used to move the argument: tables likely anchor the estimated discounting and counterfactual energy consumption; OCR did not fully expose every exhibit.
note_sections.9. Reusable writing moves:
- Best framing sentence pattern: "The efficiency gap may be real, but its size is an empirical question."
- Best transition pattern: move from observed underinvestment to structural decomposition.
- Best contribution sentence pattern: "We quantify how much myopia and imperfect competition jointly matter."
- Best limitation or implication move: "Policy should be calibrated to the size of the gap, not its existence alone."
note_sections.10. Memory update:
- Durable economics-writing principle: do not stop at identifying a gap; measure its magnitude.
- Durable structural-model principle: compare the observed market to a benchmark that separates behavior from structure.
- Reusable empirical design idea: decompose a policy problem into behavioral and market-power components.

ndon School of Economics and Political Science, London,

Matthieu Glachant, MINES ParisTech and PSL – Research University, Paris, 
France* 
Magnus Söderberg, University of Gothenburg, Sweden 
 
 
Abstract 
The empirical literature on the energy efficiency gap concentrates on demand 
inefficiencies in the energy-using durables markets and finds evidence that 
consumers underestimate future energy costs when purchasing a new 
appliance. We take a broader view and also consider the impact of imperfect 
competition. Using data on the UK refrigerator market (2002-2007), we find 
that the average energy consumption of appliances sold during this period was 
only 7.2% higher than what would have been observed under a scenario with a 
perfectly competitive market and non-myopic consumers. One reason for this 
small gap is that market power actually reduces energy use. 
Keywords: Energy Efficiency; Electricity Prices; Consumer Myopia; 
Imperfect Competition. 
JEL Classification: D12, L68, Q

note_sections.1. One-paragraph thesis:
- The paper estimates how much European car buyers value future fuel savings.
- It finds that consumers are somewhat myopic, but not extremely so: they pay about EUR 0.91 upfront for each EUR 1 of discounted future fuel savings.
- The policy implication is subtle: if myopia were stronger, the ranking of fuel taxes versus other policies would look different.
note_sections.2. Story ladder:
- Real-world tension or puzzle: fuel taxes affect both emissions and private car-buying decisions.
- Why the puzzle matters now: policy design depends on whether consumers internalize future fuel costs.
- What the literature already explains: buyers may underweight operating costs, especially for durable goods.
- What is still missing or weakly identified: a direct estimate of fuel-cost valuation in the car market.
- The paper's move: infer consumer discounting from observed European vehicle choices.
- Main payoff: observed myopia is limited enough that tax-policy conclusions are not one-sided.
note_sections.3. Model or identification core:
- Research design type: structural demand estimation with policy counterfactuals.
- Structural model class or reduced-form design: car-choice model with purchase price and discounted fuel cost.
- Key equations or choice objects: consumer utility from vehicle attributes, upfront price, and expected fuel expense.
- Endogeneity problem: fuel economy, price, and taxes are jointly determined with product design and market positioning.
- Identification strategy: recover marginal willingness to pay for future fuel savings from observed market choices.
- What assumptions are doing the heavy lifting: the discounting structure and stable preferences over fuel costs.
note_sections.4. Data and measurement:
- Unit of observation: vehicle models / car-market choices.
- Market definition: European car market.
- Main dependent variable: vehicle choice and implied willingness to pay for fuel savings.
- Core explanatory variables: purchase price, fuel cost, emissions-related taxes, and vehicle attributes.
- Instruments / moments / shocks: not fully extracted from OCR; likely product-market moments and tax variation.
- Important sample restrictions: European car market only; the precise countries and years were not fully recoverable from OCR.
note_sections.5. Findings and mechanisms:
- Baseline result: consumers value future fuel savings at about EUR 0.91 per EUR 1 discounted value.
- Mechanism evidence: there is myopia, but it is modest rather than extreme.
- Heterogeneity evidence: policy consequences depend on how much stronger myopia is in counterfactuals.
- Welfare or counterfactual result: if consumers were more myopic, fuel-tax rankings across policies could reverse.
- Limits the authors admit: the policy ranking is sensitive to the estimated degree of behavioral bias.
note_sections.6. Contribution construction:
- Which papers are treated as the nearest neighbors: consumer myopia, fuel economy, and environmental tax policy papers.
- What exact gap the authors claim: prior work often assumes discounting rather than estimating it in market data.
- How the introduction stages novelty: by tying fuel-cost valuation directly to tax policy in the vehicle market.
- Whether the contribution is data, method, theory, policy, or a combination: mostly structural estimation plus policy design insight.
note_sections.7. Literature review function:
- Where the review sits: early introduction before the model.
- How the review is organized: myopia, vehicle choice, and tax-policy effects.
- Which citations do positioning work: consumer-bias and vehicle-demand studies.
- Which citations do method-validation work: structural demand and durable-goods valuation papers.
note_sections.8. Writing structure map:
- Introduction move sequence: policy puzzle -> behavioral hypothesis -> estimation strategy -> quantitative result -> policy implication.
- Section order: background, model, data, estimation, counterfactuals, conclusion.
- Where the paper turns from setup to payoff: once the EUR 0.91 valuation estimate is established.
- How tables/figures are used to move the argument: tables likely show valuation estimates and policy rankings; OCR extraction was clear enough on the main numbers but not on every exhibit.
note_sections.9. Reusable writing moves:
- Best framing sentence pattern: "Policy conclusions depend on how consumers discount future operating costs."
- Best transition pattern: move from individual choice bias to tax design.
- Best contribution sentence pattern: "We estimate the money value consumers place on future fuel savings."
- Best limitation or implication move: "If the behavioral parameter were larger, the policy ranking would change."
note_sections.10. Memory update:
- Durable economics-writing principle: quantify the behavioral parameter that policy debates usually treat as given.
- Durable structural-model principle: fuel-cost valuation can be inferred from durable-goods choice if the discounting structure is explicit.
- Reusable empirical design idea: connect micro-level discounting estimates to environmental tax policy.
- Follow-up paper to pair with this one: a study on how fuel taxes alter vehicle substitution when discounting is heterogeneous.

27_lxuzm7vx.title: What does an electric vehicle replace?
27_lxuzm7vx.journal: Journal of Environmental Economics and Management

apa_citation.reference: Xing, J., Leard, B., & Li, S. (2021). What does an electric vehicle replace?. Journal of Environmental Economics and Management. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jeem.2021.102432

note_sections.1. One-paragraph thesis:
- The paper asks what vehicles EVs actually replace, because emissions benefits depend on the substitute, not just on the new EV sale.
- Its answer is that replacement is non-random and EVs often displace gasoline cars with above-average fuel economy.
- The payoff is a more realistic emissions accounting and a better basis for subsidy design.
note_sections.2. Story ladder:
- Real-world tension or puzzle: an EV policy can look good on adoption counts while still replacing relatively efficient gasoline cars.
- Why the puzzle matters now: emissions policy needs counterfactual replacement, not just sales growth.
- What the literature already explains: many studies estimate EV adoption, but fewer infer the full substitution matrix.
- What is still missing or weakly identified: the mapping from an EV purchase to the gasoline car it replaces.
- The paper's move: estimate a random-coefficients demand model with second-choice data and counterfactual removal of EVs.
- Main payoff: emissions benefits are smaller than naive replacement assumptions would imply.
note_sections.3. Model or identification core:
- Research design type: structural demand estimation with counterfactual simulation.
- Structural model class or reduced-form design: random-coefficients discrete choice model.
- Key equations or choice objects: vehicle demand, substitution patterns, and cross-price elasticities.
- Endogeneity problem: substitution is not random, and simple replacement assumptions are too coarse.
- Identification strategy: combine household survey data, vehicle characteristics, registrations, and second-choice information.
- What assumptions are doing the heavy lifting: the demand system and the interpretation of reported second choices.
note_sections.4. Data and measurement:
- Unit of observation: household vehicle choice / market share information.
- Market definition: US new-vehicle market with EV alternatives.
- Main dependent variable: vehicle choice and implied replacement pattern.
- Core explanatory variables: vehicle price, characteristics, EV availability, and fuel economy.
- Instruments / moments / shocks: the counterfactual is built from the estimated demand system rather than a quasi-experimental shock.
- Important sample restrictions: some EV models lack substitute-choice data, and the paper notes this limitation.
note_sections.5. Findings and mechanisms:
- Baseline result: EVs replace gasoline cars with higher-than-average fuel economy.
- Mechanism evidence: second-choice data show that many EV buyers were also considering hybrids or plug-in hybrids.
- Heterogeneity evidence: the replacement pattern differs across EV models and consumer groups.
- Welfare or counterfactual result: ignoring non-random replacement overstates emissions benefits; the paper also compares the current uniform subsidy with alternatives that induce more incremental EV purchases.
- Limits the authors admit: some EV models are missing substitute-choice data, so exact replacement shares are not equally precise everywhere.
note_sections.6. Contribution construction:

note_sections.1. One-paragraph thesis:
- The paper studies attribute-based regulation, where the stringency of a standard depends on a secondary characteristic of the regulated object.
- Its answer is that this policy form can generate distortion, bunching, and welfare tradeoffs that are not visible in a simple flat standard.
- The contribution is both theoretical and empirical: a framework plus evidence from Japanese weight-based fuel-economy rules.
note_sections.2. Story ladder:
- Real-world tension or puzzle: fuel-economy regulations often tie the target to vehicle weight or another attribute.
- Why the puzzle matters now: policymakers use attribute-based rules widely, but their welfare consequences are not transparent.
- What the literature already explains: conventional standards and taxes are better understood than attribute-based designs.
- What is still missing or weakly identified: a unified way to map the extra attribute into welfare and behavior.
- The paper's move: build a theory of attribute-based regulation and then test its predictions with bunching and a policy change.
- Main payoff: a clearer guide to when attribute basing is useful and when it is mainly distortionary.
note_sections.3. Model or identification core:
- Research design type: theory plus quasi-experimental evidence.
- Structural model class or reduced-form design: welfare model of attribute-based regulation, plus empirical bunching and counterfactual estimation.
- Key equations or choice objects: the regulation is a function of the target attribute and the secondary attribute.
- Endogeneity problem: regulated agents may sort or bunch around thresholds, and the attribute itself may change response to policy.
- Identification strategy: bunching around notches plus a policy change to estimate response and welfare implications.
- What assumptions are doing the heavy lifting: the mapping from observed bunching to behavioral responses and the maintained structure of the welfare model.
note_sections.4. Data and measurement:
- Unit of observation: vehicles around the regulated threshold.
- Market definition: the Japanese vehicle market under weight-based fuel-economy regulation.
- Main dependent variable: bunching / weight choice / fuel-economy outcome.
- Core explanatory variables: regulatory targets, vehicle weight, and secondary attributes.
- Instruments / moments / shocks: policy thresholds and a policy reform.
- Important sample restrictions: the empirical design focuses on vehicles near the relevant regulatory cutoffs.
note_sections.5. Findings and mechanisms:
- Baseline result: vehicle weight increased in response to regulation, consistent with bunching.
- Mechanism evidence: attribute basing changes the shadow value of the secondary characteristic and therefore the chosen bundle.
- Heterogeneity evidence: the welfare effect depends on the relationship between the targeted and secondary attributes.
- Welfare or counterfactual result: the paper computes welfare consequences of attribute-based policies and compares them with alternative standards.
- Limits the authors admit: exact welfare ranking depends on the parameterization and the policy environment.
note_sections.6. Contribution construction:
- Which papers are treated as the nearest neighbors: work on fuel-economy standards, regulation design, and bunching.
- What exact gap the authors claim: previous literature lacked a unified economics framework for attribute-based regulation.
- How the introduction stages novelty: define the policy form, show its prevalence, then explain the missing theory and evidence.
- Whether the contribution is data, method, theory, policy, or a combination: theory plus policy evaluation, with an empirical check.
note_sections.7. Literature review function:
- Where the review sits: the introduction and setup sections.
- How the review is organized: by policy design problem, especially why the secondary attribute matters.
- Which citations do positioning work: fuel-economy regulation papers and attribute-based policy examples show the policy relevance.
- Which citations do method-validation work: bunching and tax-function literature justify the empirical approach.
note_sections.8. Writing structure map:
- Introduction move sequence: policy form -> prevalence -> missing framework -> empirical strategy -> welfare result.
- Section order: intro -> theory -> empirical setting -> bunching -> estimation -> counterfactuals -> conclusion.
- Where the paper turns from setup to payoff: once the theory identifies the key parameters and the bunching evidence appears.
- How tables/figures are used to move the argument: threshold plots and counterfactual tables are the natural bridge from theory to welfare.
note_sections.9. Reusable writing moves:
- Best framing sentence pattern: "The target of the regulation is not the only margin that matters."
- Best transition pattern: "We now use a simple model to pin down the welfare consequences."
- Best contribution sentence pattern: "A policy class that is common in practice deserves a theory that matches its actual design."
- Best limitation or implication move: make the welfare ranking conditional on the correlation between the target and the secondary attribute.
note_sections.10. Memory update:
- Durable economics-writing principle: define the policy class by its actual administrative rule, not by a simplified label.
- Durable structural-model principle: a secondary attribute can change both incentives and welfare in ways a flat standard cannot capture.
- Reusable empirical design idea: bunching at cutoffs is the right lens for attribute-based rules.
- Follow-up paper to pair with this one: any regulation paper where the policy index depends on another characteristic.

20_bwi7cwgm.theory_design_memory:
- The paper studies attribute-based regulation, where the stringency of a standard depends on a secondary characteristic of the regulated object.
- Its answer is that this policy form can generate distortion, bunching, and welfare tradeoffs that are not visible in a simple flat standard.
- The contribution is both theoretical and empirical: a framework plus evidence from Japanese weight-based fuel-economy rules.

- Real-world tension or puzzle: fuel-economy regulations often tie the target to vehicle weight or another attribute.
- Why the puzzle matters now: policymakers use attribute-based rules widely, but their welfare consequences are not transparent.
- What the literature already explains: conventional standards and taxes are better understood than attribute-based designs.
- What is still missing or weakly identified: a unified way to map the extra attribute into welfare and behavior.
- The paper's move: build a theory of attribute-based regulation and then test its predictions with bunching and a policy change.
- Main payoff: a clearer guide to when attribute basing is useful and when it is mainly distortionary.

- Research design type: theory plus quasi-experimental evidence.
- Structural model class or reduced-form design: welfare model of attribute-based regulation, plus empirical bunching and counterfactual estimation.
- Key equations or choice objects: the regulation is a function of the target attribute and the secondary attribute.
- Endogeneity problem: regulated agents may sort or bunch around thresholds, and the attribute itself may change response to policy.
- Identification strategy: bunching around notches plus a policy change to estimate response and welfare implications.
- What assumptions are doing the heavy lifting: the mapping from observed bunching to behavioral responses and the maintained structure of the welfare model.

- Unit of observation: vehicles around the regulated threshold.
- Market definition: the Japanese vehicle market under weight-based fuel-economy regulation.
- Main dependent variable: bunching / weight choice / fuel-economy outcome.
- Core explanatory variables: regulatory targets, vehicle weight, and secondary attributes.
- Instruments / moments / shocks: policy thresholds and a policy reform.
- Important sample restrictions: the empirical design focuses on vehicles near the relevant regulatory cutoffs.

- Which papers are treated as the nearest neighbors: work on fuel-economy standards, regulation design, and bunching.
- What exact gap the authors claim: previous literature lacked a unified economics framework for attribute-based regulation.
- How the introduction stages novelty: define the policy form, show its prevalence, then explain the missing theory and evidence.
- Whether the contribution is data, method, theory, policy, or a combination: theory plus policy evaluation, with an empirical check.

- Where the review sits: the introduction and setup sections.
- How the review is organized: by policy design problem, especially why the secondary attribute matters.
- Which citations do positioning work: fuel-economy regulation papers and attribute-based policy examples show the policy relevance.
- Which citations do method-validation work: bunching and tax-function literature justify the empirical approach.

intro.snippet:
Abstract
We study “attribute-based regulations,” under which regulatory compliance of a ﬁrm,
product, or individual depends upon a secondary attribute that is not the intended
target of the regulation. We develop a theoretical model of the welfare consequences
of attribute basing, including its distortionary costs and potential beneﬁts. We then
quantify these welfare consequences using quasi-experimental evidence from weight-
based fuel-economy regulations. We use bunching analysis to show that vehicle weight
increased in response to regulation. We also leverage a policy change and develop a
new method for analyzing “double-notched” policies to compare the costs and beneﬁts
of a speciﬁc attribute-based policy.
Keywords:
fuel-economy standards, energy eﬃciency, corrective taxation, notches,

data.snippet:
ing. To do so, we analyze Japanese fuel-economy regu-
lations, under which ﬁrms making heavier cars are allowed to have lower fuel economy. The
Japanese regulation oﬀers two empirical advantages over data from other markets, including
automobile markets in the E.U. and U.S. First, the Japanese regulations have existed for
more than three decades and have experienced several policy reforms. Second, the Japanese
ABR is notched—the fuel economy required for a given vehicle is a decreasing step function
of its weight. Automakers therefore have a large incentive to increase vehicle weight only up
to key thresholds where the mandated fuel economy drops discretely. These notches do not
change the fundamental economic incentives at play, but they aid empirical identiﬁcation.
Our panel analysis diﬀers from existing work in this area by considering a double notch (i.e.,
a notch in two coordinates), which is, to the best of our knowledge, new to the literature.1

Conclusion
This paper shows that attribute-based regulation is an imperfect substitute for ﬂat policies
with compliance trading. The key drawback to attribute basing is that it creates distor-
tions in the attribute, and we show that those distortions are greater when the attribute is
more responsive to policy. Empirically we demonstrate that those distortions are substan-
tial for the case of weight-based fuel-economy regulations in Japan. Attribute basing may
have appeal when it is used to achieve distributional goals, or when compliance trading is
unavailable. Regarding the latter, for the Japanese tax policy we consider, attribute basing
is signiﬁcantly more eﬃcient than a ﬂat standard without trading, but it is twice as costly
as a ﬂat standard with compliance trading.

Benjamin Leard∗ Resources for the Future

June 2017
Abstract
During historical periods in which US fuel economy standards were unchanging, automakers increased performance but not fuel economy, contrasting with recent periods of tightening standards and rising fuel economy. This paper evaluates the welfare consequences of automakers forgoing performance increases to raise fuel economy as standards have tightened since 2012. Using a unique data set and a novel approach to account for fuel economy and performance endogeneity, we find undervaluation of fuel cost savings and high valuation of performance. Welfare costs of forgone performance approximately equal expected fuel savings benefits, suggesting approximately zero net private consumer benefit from tightened standards.

note_sections.1. One-paragraph thesis:
- The paper evaluates a mandatory energy-label policy in the Brazilian refrigerator market.
- Its result is that labels modestly raise valuation for efficiency, but do not fully close the efficiency gap.
- The main lesson is that information policy can move demand, yet equilibrium sorting across products may remain weak.
note_sections.2. Story ladder:
- Real-world tension or puzzle: energy labels are supposed to help consumers reward efficient products.
- Why the puzzle matters now: if labels barely change choices, disclosure policy may be too weak to deliver energy savings.
- What the literature already explains: labels can affect attention, valuation, and product selection.
- What is still missing or weakly identified: market-level evidence on how a real labeling mandate changes demand.
- The paper's move: study the Brazilian refrigerator label program.
- Main payoff: labels help, but not enough to eliminate the gap or trigger large switching.
note_sections.3. Model or identification core:
- Research design type: policy evaluation / demand response analysis.
- Structural model class or reduced-form design: market-demand analysis around a labeling intervention.
- Key equations or choice objects: consumer valuation of product energy efficiency and other refrigerator attributes.
- Endogeneity problem: label adoption is policy-driven, but product portfolios and demand responses are endogenous.
- Identification strategy: exploit the policy change to compare consumer response before and after labeling.
- What assumptions are doing the heavy lifting: comparability of demand environments and stable product characteristics apart from the policy.
note_sections.4. Data and measurement:
- Unit of observation: refrigerator products and market choices.
- Market definition: Brazilian refrigerator market.
- Main dependent variable: valuation and choice response to efficiency labels.
- Core explanatory variables: label presence, energy efficiency, and product characteristics.
- Instruments / moments / shocks: the label mandate itself is the key policy shock.
- Important sample restrictions: refrigerator market only; OCR extraction was noisy in some spots, so exact sample design may need verification against the PDF if used in a formal writeup.
note_sections.5. Findings and mechanisms:
- Baseline result: mandatory labels modestly increase mean valuation for efficient products.
- Mechanism evidence: information improves product evaluation, but does not create dramatic switching.
- Heterogeneity evidence: the distribution of valuations does not become equalized across products.
- Welfare or counterfactual result: the policy cannot eliminate the energy-efficiency gap on its own.
- Limits the authors admit: the effect size is modest, so labels are not a full substitute for stronger policy.

- Which papers are treated as the nearest neighbors: energy-labeling and appliance-demand papers.

A B S T R A C T
The PBE program made the adoption of energy labels mandatory in the Brazilian refrigerator market. In this
paper, we examine the effects of PBE using data from a nationally representative sample of households and
a structural model of appliance choice. We document a modest increase in the valuation of energy costs by
Brazilian consumers. However, the program is unable to eliminate the energy efficiency gap, in that consumers
undervalue energy costs both pre-and post-PBE. Moreover, our policy simulation documents little product
switching and heterogeneity in responses. All in all, while the PBE program aimed to both reduce energy
consumption and increase energy efficiency, we can only claim robust evidence of the latter.

ABSTRACT
While China has made great strides in transforming its centrally-planned economy to a marketoriented economy, there still exist widespread interregional trade barriers, such as policies and practices that protect local firms against competition from non-local firms. This study documents the presence of local protectionism and quantifies its impacts on market competition and social welfare in the context of China’s automobile market. This market exhibits a salient feature that vehicle models by joint ventures (JVs) and especially state-owned enterprises (SOEs) command much higher market shares in their headquarter province than at the national level. Counterfactual simulations show that local protection leads to significant choice distortions, resulting in 18.7 billion yuan of consumer welfare loss, amounting to 40% of total subsidy. nterregional barriers to trade that limit the mobility of goods and services. These barriers impede market integration and could lead to substantial welfare losses (Donaldson, 2015). One such barrier results from policies and practices that protect local firms against competition from non-local firms, which we characterize as local protectionism. Local protectionism arises from a combination of factors: the top-down political personnel system that relies heavily on local GDP growth for promotion, rent-seeking behaviour of local officials who are closely connected to local SOEs or JVs, and the lack of effective regulations from the central government.
Local protectionism in China takes many forms, including explicit discounts for local brands and implicit barriers for non-local brands. Our analysis provides the following three key findings that are robust across various specifications and sample cuts. 01_jdv2eev6.title: Better Lucky Than Rich? Welfare Analysis of Automobile Licence Allocations in Beijing and Shanghai

apa_citation.reference: Li, S. (2018). Better Lucky Than Rich? Welfare Analysis of Automobile Licence Allocations in Beijing and Shanghai. The Review of Economic Studies. https://doi.org/10.1093/restud/rdx067

note_sections.1. One-paragraph thesis:
- The paper asks how much welfare is lost when a city restricts car ownership with a lottery rather than a uniform-price auction.
- Its answer is that Beijing's lottery design creates large misallocation costs, even though it lowers some externalities relative to pure market allocation.
- The key takeaway is that "fair" allocation can be much more expensive than it looks once households differ in willingness to pay and usage intensity.
note_sections.2. Story ladder:
- Real-world tension or puzzle: Beijing and Shanghai both ration car licenses, but they use very different allocation rules.
- Why the puzzle matters now: when quantity controls are unavoidable, the allocation rule itself becomes a major policy lever.
- What the literature already explains: car ownership regulation can reduce congestion and pollution, but not the welfare ranking of allocation mechanisms.

note_sections.1. One-paragraph thesis:
- The paper estimates how BEV specifications, prices, and incentives affect consumer choice in Norway.
- Its answer is that a BLP-style random-coefficients discrete choice model can capture heterogeneous consumers and the role of different incentive components.
- The practical payoff is a more policy-relevant picture of which BEV attributes and incentives matter for adoption.
note_sections.2. Story ladder:
- Real-world tension or puzzle: Norway has strong EV incentives, but adoption still varies by model, consumer type, and use case.
- Why the puzzle matters now: policies interact with charging, taxation, road access, and vehicle characteristics.
- What the literature already explains: simpler demand models can miss heterogeneity and multi-attribute choice.
- What is still missing or weakly identified: a model that simultaneously handles specs, prices, and incentives across consumer groups.
- The paper's move: use a BLP framework on Norwegian market data.
- Main payoff: the paper can speak to both policy design and marketing strategy.
note_sections.3. Model or identification core:
- Research design type: structural demand estimation.
- Structural model class or reduced-form design: BLP random-coefficients discrete choice model.
- Key equations or choice objects: consumer utility over BEV models, attributes, prices, and incentive exposure.
- Endogeneity problem: prices and product characteristics can be correlated with unobserved quality.
- Identification strategy: random coefficients with market-level variation and observed heterogeneity in income and purchase purpose.
- What assumptions are doing the heavy lifting: the utility specification and the interpretation of heterogeneity in preferences.
note_sections.4. Data and measurement:
- Unit of observation: Norwegian BEV choice data by market and model.
- Market definition: Norway BEV market.
- Main dependent variable: BEV choice / market share.
- Core explanatory variables: car specifications, prices, and incentive measures.
- Instruments / moments / shocks: the paper uses the BLP-style moment structure; exact instruments are not fully extracted here.
- Important sample restrictions: the paper notes that it cannot model the full BEV-versus-ICE choice set because regular vehicle sales data are unavailable.
note_sections.5. Findings and mechanisms:
- Baseline result: BEV specifications and incentives have meaningful positive effects on choice.
- Mechanism evidence: heterogeneity matters by income level and purchase purpose, including individual versus business use.
- Heterogeneity evidence: consumers do not respond to incentives in a one-size-fits-all way.
- Welfare or counterfactual result: the paper is mainly a demand-side policy input rather than a full welfare analysis.
- Limits the authors admit: the outside option is limited because the data do not fully observe regular vehicle sales.
note_sections.6. Contribution construction:
- Which papers are treated as the nearest neighbors: EV demand papers and discrete-choice work on vehicle adoption.
- What exact gap the authors claim: there is little evidence on how BEV incentives interact with consumer heterogeneity in Norway.
- How the introduction stages novelty: policy-rich context -> data limitation -> need for a choice model -> heterogeneity payoff.
- Whether the contribution is data, method, theory, policy, or a combination: mostly method and policy application.
note_sections.7. Literature review function:
- Where the review sits: introduction and early empirical motivation.
- How the review is organized: by modeling approach and the limits of simpler specifications.
- Which citations do positioning work: EV adoption and consumer choice papers show what prior work misses.
- Which citations do method-validation work: discrete-choice and BLP references justify the estimation design.
note_sections.8. Writing structure map:
- Introduction move sequence: policy-rich market -> heterogeneity problem -> data constraint -> BLP solution.
- Section order: intro -> model -> data -> estimation -> results -> policy discussion.
- Where the paper turns from setup to payoff: once the paper translates attributes and incentives into estimated heterogeneity.
- How tables/figures are used to move the argument: market-share and coefficient tables likely anchor the consumer-heterogeneity story.
note_sections.9. Reusable writing moves:
- Best framing sentence pattern: "The policy question is not just whether incentives work, but for whom and through which vehicle attributes."
- Best transition pattern: "We next replace a simple logit with a random-coefficients model."
- Best contribution sentence pattern: "A better demand model lets policy speak to product design."
- Best limitation or implication move: state clearly when the dataset forces you to leave out the full outside option.
note_sections.10. Memory update:
- Durable economics-writing principle: if consumer response differs by use case, make that heterogeneity part of the main model.
- Durable structural-model principle: BLP is most useful when product attributes and unobserved quality both matter.
- Reusable empirical design idea: policy design papers can be strengthened by explicit consumer segmentation.
- Follow-up paper to pair with this one: any BLP-style EV paper with richer counterfactual supply structure.

1. Introduction
Electric vehicles (EV) convert roughly 60% of the electrical energy from the power grid to wheels, compared to 20% from
gasoline to wheels for a regular gasoline car (Department of Energy, 2014). In addition, EVs have no singular required energy
source as most internal combustion engines have, since electricity can be produced from a multitude of sources, allowing for
a diversiﬁcation of energy sources in transportation. Signiﬁcant energy/emission savings and ﬂexibility offered by EVs call for
increasing EV adoption all over the world. However, EVs have limitations compared to their internal combustion engine
counterparts. The barriers to their adoption are that, to name a few, EVs are more expensive, have limited ranges and have
less infrastructure support.

apa_citation.reference: Holland, S. P., Mansur, E. T., & Yates, A. J. (2021). The Electric Vehicle Transition and the Economics of Banning Gasoline Vehicles. American Economic Journal: Economic Policy. https://doi.org/10.1257/pol.20200120

note_sections.1. One-paragraph thesis:
- The paper studies the transition from gasoline vehicles to electric vehicles with a dynamic model.
- Its answer is that static adoption models miss the path-dependence of fleet transition, but a calibrated dynamic model suggests the inefficiency from current policy is modest.
- The practical payoff is a comparison of subsidies, bans, and bankable production quotas, with the quota often looking like the smallest deadweight loss option.
note_sections.2. Story ladder:
- Real-world tension or puzzle: EV transition policy is not just about one purchase decision; it is about a changing fleet.
- Why the puzzle matters now: gasoline vehicles impose flows of emissions, while EV costs and damages change over time.
- What the literature already explains: static models explain adoption, but not transition dynamics.
- What is still missing or weakly identified: a model that lets costs, damages, and substitution evolve over time.
- The paper's move: build and calibrate a dynamic model of the EV transition to the US market.
- Main payoff: compare policy instruments in a setting where timing and transition path matter.
note_sections.3. Model or identification core:
- Research design type: dynamic structural model.
- Structural model class or reduced-form design: dynamic transition model with declining EV production costs and potentially declining damages.
- Key equations or choice objects: vehicle replacement, adoption timing, and dynamic welfare.
- Endogeneity problem: the transition path itself changes the future state of the market.
- Identification strategy: calibration to observed US market conditions and simulation of counterfactual policies.
- What assumptions are doing the heavy lifting: the dynamic law of motion for costs, damages, and substitution.
note_sections.4. Data and measurement:
- Unit of observation: vehicle transition over time, calibrated to the US market.
- Market definition: the US light-vehicle market.
- Main dependent variable: EV adoption and welfare over the transition path.
- Core explanatory variables: EV costs, gasoline vehicle attributes, damages, and policy interventions.
- Instruments / moments / shocks: calibration moments rather than quasi-experimental shocks.
- Important sample restrictions: the model is intentionally focused on the transition margin, not a full micro demand system.
note_sections.5. Findings and mechanisms:
- Baseline result: the inefficiency of the current transition path is modest in the calibration.
- Mechanism evidence: falling costs and the timing of substitution matter more than a one-period static snapshot.
- Heterogeneity evidence: the model can be extended to endogenous substitutability and learning.
- Welfare or counterfactual result: a bankable gasoline-vehicle production quota can have the smallest deadweight loss among the compared policies.
- Limits the authors admit: calibration-based results depend on the assumed transition technology and market environment.
note_sections.6. Contribution construction:
- Which papers are treated as the nearest neighbors: static EV adoption models and dynamic adoption papers.
- What exact gap the authors claim: static models are poorly suited to study fleet transition and policy timing.
- How the introduction stages novelty: first the transition problem, then why static models fail, then the dynamic solution.
- Whether the contribution is data, method, theory, policy, or a combination: dynamic theory plus policy comparison.
note_sections.7. Literature review function:
- Where the review sits: early in the introduction.
- How the review is organized: by the limitation of static models and the need for dynamic transition analysis.
- Which citations do positioning work: prior EV adoption and green-technology transition papers define the gap.
- Which citations do method-validation work: papers on dynamic vehicle adoption and replacement support the model class.
note_sections.8. Writing structure map:
- Introduction move sequence: static-limit argument -> dynamic alternative -> calibration -> policy ranking.
- Section order: intro -> model -> calibration -> welfare and policy comparisons -> extensions -> conclusion.
- Where the paper turns from setup to payoff: once the model is calibrated and the policy comparison can be simulated.
- How tables/figures are used to move the argument: transition-path plots and policy-comparison tables carry the policy conclusion.
note_sections.9. Reusable writing moves:
- Best framing sentence pattern: "A static model can miss the point when the object of interest is the transition itself."
- Best transition pattern: "We now calibrate the model to quantify the size of the inefficiency."
- Best contribution sentence pattern: "The policy ranking changes once the model tracks the fleet over time."
- Best limitation or implication move: keep the answer tied to the assumed trajectory of technological change.
note_sections.10. Memory update:
- Durable economics-writing principle: if the policy concern is a transition, write the model as a transition model.
- Durable structural-model principle: endogenous substitution and learning can materially change welfare rankings.
- Reusable empirical design idea: calibration is the right tool when the main object is a long-run policy path.
- Follow-up paper to pair with this one: any durable-good transition model with policy bans or quotas.

Winners and Losers: The Distributional Effects of the French Feebate on the Automobile Market
Short title: Winners & losers from the French feebate
Isis Durrmeyer
October 19, 2021
Abstract
I quantify the welfare and environmental gains and losses from a policy establishing an environmental tax/subsidy for new cars in France in 2008. I estimate a structural model of demand and supply that features heterogeneity in consumer preferences to go beyond the average policy effects and analyse distributional aspects. The policy reduces average carbon emissions by 1.6% at the cost of additional emissions of local pollutants. The regulation favours middle-income individuals but has redistributive effects when combined with a tax that is proportional to income. Moreover, local pollutant emissions increase least in poor and rural areas, suggesting another redistribution channel.

apa_citation.reference: Gerlagh, R., Bijgaart, I. v. d., Nijland, H., & Michielsen, T. (2018). Fiscal Policy and CO2 Emissions of New Passenger Cars in the EU. Environmental and Resource Economics. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10640-016-0067-6

note_sections.1. One-paragraph thesis:
- The paper studies how different fiscal policies change the CO2 intensity of new passenger cars in the EU.
- It finds that registration taxes with stronger CO2 sensitivity reduce emissions intensity, while fuel taxes also push toward more efficient cars.
- Annual road taxes, by contrast, have little or even adverse effect.
note_sections.2. Story ladder:
- Real-world tension or puzzle: EU countries use several car taxes, but their emissions effects are not the same.
- Why the puzzle matters now: climate policy needs to know which tax margin actually changes vehicle choices.
- What the literature already explains: car taxation should affect efficiency and fuel mix, but evidence is fragmented.
- What is still missing or weakly identified: a comparative estimate across registration, fuel, and annual taxes.
- The paper's move: evaluate those fiscal instruments in a common EU car-market framework.
- Main payoff: not all car taxes are equal; some are much better aligned with CO2 goals.
note_sections.3. Model or identification core:
- Research design type: comparative policy evaluation with market-level CO2 outcomes.
- Structural model class or reduced-form design: vehicle-choice framework linking taxes to vehicle attributes.
- Key equations or choice objects: new-car choice over emissions, fuel type, and other specifications.
- Endogeneity problem: tax regimes co-evolve with consumer demand and policy goals.
- Identification strategy: exploit cross-country and policy variation in fiscal instruments.
- What assumptions are doing the heavy lifting: comparability across markets and stable response to tax incentives.
note_sections.4. Data and measurement:
- Unit of observation: new passenger cars.
- Market definition: EU passenger-car markets.
- Main dependent variable: CO2 intensity of the average new car.
- Core explanatory variables: registration taxes, fuel taxes, and annual road taxes.
- Instruments / moments / shocks: policy variation across countries and time.
- Important sample restrictions: new cars in the EU; precise country coverage is in the paper, but the OCR read was clear on the main design.
note_sections.5. Findings and mechanisms:
- Baseline result: higher CO2-sensitivity of registration taxes reduces CO2 intensity by about 1.3%.
- Mechanism evidence: the same policy increases diesel share by about 6.5 percentage points.
- Heterogeneity evidence: higher fuel taxes also induce more efficient cars, while higher diesel fuel taxes reduce diesel share.
- Welfare or counterfactual result: annual road taxes show little or negative effect on CO2 intensity.
- Limits the authors admit: policy effects differ by tax type, so no single fiscal instrument is dominant in every context.
note_sections.6. Contribution construction:
- Which papers are treated as the nearest neighbors: vehicle-tax policy, fuel-demand, and emissions studies.
- What exact gap the authors claim: previous work has not cleanly compared the emissions effects of the full tax menu.
- How the introduction stages novelty: by focusing on fiscal policy instruments rather than a single regulation.
- Whether the contribution is data, method, theory, policy, or a combination: policy comparison with reduced-form evidence.
note_sections.7. Literature review function:
- Where the review sits: early introduction before the empirical specification.
- How the review is organized: fiscal policy, emissions outcomes, and vehicle substitution.
- Which citations do positioning work: car-tax and CO2-policy papers.
- Which citations do method-validation work: market-level vehicle-choice studies.
note_sections.8. Writing structure map:
- Introduction move sequence: emissions problem -> tax toolkit -> comparison gap -> result summary.
- Section order: policy context, empirical design, results, robustness, conclusion.
- Where the paper turns from setup to payoff: when registration taxes are shown to beat annual taxes on CO2 alignment.
- How tables/figures are used to move the argument: results tables and policy-comparison figures likely do the heavy lifting; OCR was clear on the headline estimates.
note_sections.9. Reusable writing moves:
- Best framing sentence pattern: "The question is not whether taxes matter, but which tax margin matters."
- Best transition pattern: move from policy inventory to instrument comparison.
- Best contribution sentence pattern: "We compare the emissions effects of the main fiscal tools in one market."
- Best limitation or implication move: "A tax instrument is only as good as the margin it actually changes."
note_sections.10. Memory update:
- Durable economics-writing principle: policy menus should be evaluated instrument by instrument, not as a single lump.
- Durable structural-model principle: CO2 outcomes are mediated by substitution toward fuel type and vehicle efficiency.
- Reusable empirical design idea: compare policy types that target the same market but different choice margins.
- Follow-up paper to pair with this one: a cross-country comparison of registration taxes versus feebates on vehicle emissions.

Abstract To what extent have national ﬁscal policies contributed to the decarbonisation of
newly sold passenger cars? We construct a simple model that generates predictions regarding
the effect of ﬁscal policies on average CO2 emissions of new cars, and then test the model
empirically. Our empirical strategy combines a diverse series of data. First, we use a large
database of vehicle-speciﬁc taxes in 15 EU countries over 2001–2010 to construct a measure
for the vehicle registration and annual road tax levels, and separately, for the CO2 sensitivity
of these taxes. We ﬁnd that for many countries the ﬁscal policies have become more sensitive
to CO2 emissions of new cars. We then use these constructed measures to estimate the effect
of ﬁscal policies on the CO2 emissions of the new car ﬂeet.

07_9hujhutj.title: Disentangling sources of vehicle emissions reduction in France: 2003–2008

apa_citation.reference: D’Haultfoeuille, X., Durrmeyer, I., & Février, P. (2016). Disentangling sources of vehicle emissions reduction in France: 2003–2008. International Journal of Industrial Organization. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ijindorg.2016.05.002

note_sections.1. One-paragraph thesis:
- The paper decomposes the fall in vehicle emissions in France between 2003 and 2008.
- Its main finding is that policy mattered, but not all policy instruments mattered equally.
- A large share of the emissions decline is attributed to changing preferences, while registration-tax CO2 sensitivity and feebate design also matter.
note_sections.2. Story ladder:
- Real-world tension or puzzle: emissions from new vehicles were falling, but the drivers of that decline were not obvious.
- Why the puzzle matters now: policy makers need to know whether taxes, fuel prices, or preference shifts are doing the work.
- What the literature already explains: emission outcomes respond to both fiscal policy and consumer choice.
- What is still missing or weakly identified: a source-by-source decomposition of the decline.
- The paper's move: separate the effects of registration taxes, annual taxes, fuel prices, and preference shifts.
- Main payoff: policy is important, but changing consumer preference explains a surprisingly large part of the decline.
note_sections.3. Model or identification core:
- Research design type: structural decomposition / policy attribution.
- Structural model class or reduced-form design: vehicle-choice model with emissions and tax policy.
- Key equations or choice objects: household choice among car models under tax schedules and fuel costs.
- Endogeneity problem: emissions, prices, and taxes are jointly shaped by market equilibrium.
- Identification strategy: use the structure of taxes and market variation to isolate channels.
- What assumptions are doing the heavy lifting: stable demand and correct mapping from policy to vehicle attributes.
note_sections.4. Data and measurement:
- Unit of observation: new passenger cars / market choices in France.
- Market definition: French vehicle market over 2003-2008.
- Main dependent variable: vehicle emissions intensity.
- Core explanatory variables: registration taxes, annual taxes, feebate incentives, and fuel prices.
- Instruments / moments / shocks: tax schedule variation and market shares.
- Important sample restrictions: French new-car market during the study window; OCR gave the broad design more clearly than every data detail.
note_sections.5. Findings and mechanisms:
- Baseline result: registration taxes that are more CO2-sensitive reduce CO2 intensity, with a reported elasticity of about 0.1% per 1% increase.
- Mechanism evidence: feebate design has a crowding-in effect, suggesting policy can shift the composition of purchases.
- Heterogeneity evidence: annual taxes have little effect, so not all recurring taxes work the same way.
- Welfare or counterfactual result: changing preferences accounts for roughly 40% of the overall emissions decline.
- Limits the authors admit: the decomposition depends on the quality of the structural attribution, so some channel shares are model-based rather than directly observed.
note_sections.6. Contribution construction:
- Which papers are treated as the nearest neighbors: vehicle emissions policy, tax design, and car-demand papers.
- What exact gap the authors claim: prior work measures policy effects, but not the share of decline due to each source.
- How the introduction stages novelty: it frames the paper as a decomposition of a real observed emissions reduction.
- Whether the contribution is data, method, theory, policy, or a combination: policy decomposition plus structural estimation.
note_sections.7. Literature review function:
- Where the review sits: in the introduction before the decomposition exercise.
- How the review is organized: tax policy, fuel costs, consumer choice, and emissions outcomes.
- Which citations do positioning work: car taxation and emissions-control papers.
- Which citations do method-validation work: structural auto-demand and policy-counterfactual studies.
note_sections.8. Writing structure map:
- Introduction move sequence: emissions decline -> attribution puzzle -> decomposition strategy -> main shares.
- Section order: policy context, model, data, estimation, decomposition results, conclusion.
- Where the paper turns from setup to payoff: when it separates preference change from tax effects.
- How tables/figures are used to move the argument: tables likely show channel shares and policy elasticities; OCR was sufficient for the headline numbers but not for every exhibit label.
note_sections.9. Reusable writing moves:
- Best framing sentence pattern: "When an outcome moves, the key question is which channel moved it."
- Best transition pattern: move from aggregate trend to channel decomposition.
- Best contribution sentence pattern: "We disentangle the sources of the emissions decline."
- Best limitation or implication move: "Policy design matters, but demand-side preference shifts can be just as important."
note_sections.10. Memory update:
- Durable economics-writing principle: decomposition is stronger than correlation when multiple policy channels move together.
- Durable structural-model principle: taxes should be interpreted through the choice margin they actually move.
- Reusable empirical design idea: build a policy attribution exercise around a real observed aggregate decline.
- Follow-up paper to pair with this one: a study that decomposes CO2 reductions into pricing, technology, and preference channels in another market.

apa_citation.reference: Miravete, E. J., Moral, M. J., & Thurk, J. (2018). Fuel taxation, emissions policy, and competitive advantage in the diffusion of European diesel automobiles. The RAND Journal of Economics. https://doi.org/10.1111/1756-2171.12243

note_sections.1. One-paragraph thesis:
- The paper argues that fuel-tax and emissions policies helped diffuse diesel vehicles in Europe.
- It shows that those policies favored diesel in ways that also acted like non-tariff trade barriers.
- The policy implication is that environmental rules can generate competitive effects that look like protectionism.
note_sections.2. Story ladder:
- Real-world tension or puzzle: diesel diffusion was not just a technology story; policy was shaping relative advantage.
- Why the puzzle matters now: climate and trade policy often interact in hidden ways.
- What the literature already explains: fuel taxes and emissions policy can change vehicle mix.
- What is still missing or weakly identified: a structural estimate of the trade-policy equivalent of those effects.
- The paper's move: use a structural model to translate policy-induced diesel diffusion into NTB equivalents.
- Main payoff: emissions policy can function like an implicit trade barrier.
note_sections.3. Model or identification core:
- Research design type: structural trade and diffusion analysis.
- Structural model class or reduced-form design: diffusion model with competitive advantage in vehicle adoption.
- Key equations or choice objects: adoption of diesel automobiles across European markets.
- Endogeneity problem: policy, technology, and market share co-evolve.
- Identification strategy: estimate a structural model of diffusion and map policy changes into tariff equivalents.
- What assumptions are doing the heavy lifting: model-based translation from policy effects to trade barriers.
note_sections.4. Data and measurement:
- Unit of observation: European automobile diffusion / market shares.
- Market definition: European diesel automobile market.
- Main dependent variable: diesel diffusion and relative market advantage.
- Core explanatory variables: fuel taxes, emissions policy, and policy-induced cost differences.
- Instruments / moments / shocks: not fully extracted from OCR; the main variation is policy and market diffusion patterns.
- Important sample restrictions: European diesel diffusion context; exact country sample should be checked if used in replication.
note_sections.5. Findings and mechanisms:
- Baseline result: fuel taxation and emissions policy favored diesel vehicles.
- Mechanism evidence: policies altered relative costs and competitive advantage across powertrains.
- Heterogeneity evidence: the effect is strongest where tax and emissions policy align.
- Welfare or counterfactual result: the implied nontariff trade policy effect is equivalent to an import tariff two to three times the official rate.
- Limits the authors admit: the NTB translation is model-based, so the equivalence is an interpretation of the structural estimates.
note_sections.6. Contribution construction:
- Which papers are treated as the nearest neighbors: diesel diffusion, fuel taxation, and trade-policy studies.
- What exact gap the authors claim: prior work has not measured the NTB content of emissions policy.
- How the introduction stages novelty: it ties environmental regulation to competitive advantage and trade effects.
- Whether the contribution is data, method, theory, policy, or a combination: structural method plus policy interpretation.
note_sections.7. Literature review function:
- Where the review sits: in the introduction and context sections.
- How the review is organized: diesel diffusion, fuel taxes, emissions policy, and trade analogies.
- Which citations do positioning work: car technology diffusion and taxation papers.
- Which citations do method-validation work: structural trade and adoption models.
note_sections.8. Writing structure map:
- Introduction move sequence: policy-induced diffusion -> competitive advantage -> trade-equivalent implication.
- Section order: background, model, estimation, results, counterfactual interpretation, conclusion.
- Where the paper turns from setup to payoff: when policy effects are recast as tariff equivalents.
- How tables/figures are used to move the argument: diffusion patterns and policy-comparison tables likely carry the evidence; OCR was clear on the main equivalence claim.
note_sections.9. Reusable writing moves:
- Best framing sentence pattern: "An environmental policy can also be a market-access policy."
- Best transition pattern: move from diffusion pattern to competitive interpretation.
- Best contribution sentence pattern: "We quantify the trade-policy equivalent of emissions policy."
- Best limitation or implication move: "A policy's effect on technology choice can reshape competitive advantage."
note_sections.10. Memory update:
- Durable economics-writing principle: policy can be evaluated in adjacent domains, not just the domain it targets.
- Durable structural-model principle: diffusion models are useful when policy changes market share over time.
- Reusable empirical design idea: translate environmental policy effects into trade-equivalent units.
- Follow-up paper to pair with this one: a study on fuel-economy standards as hidden industrial policy.
